Course · Whole course on one page

t27 basics: the language in 27 lessons

Before the FPGA course: what a t27 spec is, how the compiler reads it, and what it gives back. Every lesson opens one table or diagram drawn from its own spec and one spec you can run in your browser.

Course 0, 27 lessons, one infographic and one t27 spec each: a module, constants and types, functions and tests, then the compiler's stages and the 7 languages it writes. It comes before the FPGA course.

Every course is free, for everyone: no sign-up, no email, nothing to pay.

01

Module 1 · A spec file

What a .t27 file holds: a module line, prose lines and comments.

01

Lesson 1 of 27

What a spec is

You will learnWhat goes into a .t27 file and what the compiler gives back for it.

A spec is a plain text file that ends in .t27. It opens with a module line, declares values and functions, and carries test blocks that check them. The compiler, t27c, reads the file and answers with a verdict and code for 7 backends. The spec under this lesson has 2 constants and 1 test, and the site compiles it in your browser.

Try it

Open the lesson spec in the player and find its three parts: the module line, the constants, the test.

Open the interactive lesson →
02

Lesson 2 of 27

The module line

You will learnHow to write the module line, which names it accepts, and where it goes.

The module line is the keyword module, a name and a semicolon. Comment and prose lines may come before it; declarations come after. Names use letters, digits and underscores; the compiler in this site also accepts hyphens, as in tutorial-06-structs. A course spec on this site must use the module name its generator expects, so a wrong name is caught by the build and not by the compiler.

Try it

In the player, change the module name of this lesson spec and watch the verdict stay clean.

Open the interactive lesson →
03

Lesson 3 of 27

Comments and prose lines

You will learnWhere each kind of note may stand, and the one line that breaks the parser.

A line that starts with a semicolon is prose: the compiler skips the rest of the line. Prose lines stand at the top level, between declarations. Two slashes start a comment anywhere, after code or inside a test. One trap: a semicolon alone on its line is not an empty prose line, it is a parse error, and the whole spec fails. Put a word after it, or leave the line empty.

Try it

Add a line with a lone semicolon to the lesson spec in the player, read the error, then remove it.

Open the interactive lesson →
02

Module 2 · Values and types

Constants, the width of a whole number, and true, false and text.

04

Lesson 4 of 27

Constants

You will learnThe six pieces of a constant declaration and what each one does.

pub const WIDTH : u8 = 8; reads left to right: pub makes the name visible to other modules, const says the value is fixed, WIDTH is the name, u8 is the type, 8 is the value, and the semicolon ends it. Constants are what this site's test runner can check: the lesson spec declares WIDTH, HEIGHT and AREA and tests that 8 times 4 is 32.

Try it

Change AREA in the lesson spec to 33 and watch which test fails.

Open the interactive lesson →
05

Lesson 5 of 27

Whole numbers and their widths

You will learnThe integer types, their ranges, and the error a value too big for its type gets.

A u in the type name means unsigned, an i means signed, and the digits are the number of bits. u8 holds 0 to 255, u16 holds 0 to 65535, i32 holds negative numbers too. The compiler checks a constant against its type: give a u8 the value 300 and it stops with an error that says no u8 can hold 3 digits. The browser's checker is lenient elsewhere, so do not read its silence as proof.

Try it

Set BYTE_MAX to 300 in the player and read the error the compiler prints.

Open the interactive lesson →
06

Lesson 6 of 27

True, false and text

You will learnHow to declare a bool and a str, and what a test can compare them with.

A bool is true or false. A str is text in double quotes, and the text may hold characters that mean something elsewhere in t27, such as a semicolon or two slashes: inside quotes they are just text. A test compares a bool or a str with == and !=. One honest limit: the checker in this browser does not stop a str given to a u8 constant, so keep types and values matched yourself.

Try it

Change NAME in the lesson spec and fix the test so that it passes again.

Open the interactive lesson →
03

Module 3 · Arrays, trits and expressions

Lists of values, the three values of a trit, and what operators compute.

07

Lesson 7 of 27

Arrays

You will learnHow to declare an array, read an item, and which index is the last one.

An array type is the length in square brackets followed by the item type: [5]u8 is five unsigned bytes. The value lists the items in square brackets. Index 0 holds the item at the start, so in an array of 5 the last index is 4. A test reads an item with PRIMES[4]. Keep the declared length and the list in step: the checker in this browser does not catch a length that disagrees with the list.

Try it

Add a sixth prime to PRIMES, fix the length, and write an assert for index 5.

Open the interactive lesson →
08

Lesson 8 of 27

Trits: minus one, zero, one

You will learnHow a trit is written as a small signed constant and why 27 shows up everywhere.

A bit has two values; a trit has three: minus one, zero and one. The lesson spec writes them as i8 constants NEG, ZERO and POS, the way the tutorial specs of t27 do. Adding POS and NEG gives ZERO. Three trits have 3 times 3 times 3 combinations, which is 27: the number of lessons in this course and the cells of a TRI-27 word.

Try it

Write an assert that POS minus NEG equals 2, and check it passes.

Open the interactive lesson →
09

Lesson 9 of 27

Expressions

You will learnArithmetic operators and comparisons on the lesson constants, and the bool a comparison gives back.

An expression combines names and numbers with operators. With A = 17 and B = 5, A + B is 22, A - B is 12, A * B is 85, A / B is 3 because whole numbers divide without a fraction, and A % B is 2, the remainder. Comparisons give true or false. One limit of the test runner on this site: it does not read a minus sign in front of a number, so write negative values as constants.

Try it

Change B to 4 and predict each of the five results before you run the tests.

Open the interactive lesson →
04

Module 4 · Tests and functions

A test block, several small tests in one spec, and a function with typed inputs.

10

Lesson 10 of 27

A test block

You will learnHow a test block is written and what a failing assert reports.

A test block starts with the keyword test and a name, and holds assert lines in braces. Each assert takes an expression that must be true. When one is false, the report names the test and the number of the assert, for example assert #1 is false. A spec's tests are its claims about itself, which is why every course spec on this site carries some.

Try it

Break the test on purpose by changing DAYS, then read the failure line.

Open the interactive lesson →
11

Lesson 11 of 27

Many tests in one spec

You will learnWhy several small tests read better than one long one, and how the report counts them.

A spec may hold any number of test blocks. Each one checks one idea and has a name that says which. The report counts tests and asserts separately: the lesson spec has 3 tests and 5 asserts. When one fails, its name tells you which idea broke, and the other tests still report on their own ideas.

Try it

Make one of the three tests fail and check that the other two still pass.

Open the interactive lesson →
12

Lesson 12 of 27

Functions

You will learnThe two ways t27 writes a function signature, and the body with return.

fn add(a: u8, b: u8) -> u8 declares a function with two u8 inputs and a u8 result; the body in braces ends with return. The compiler also accepts the Zig style, pub fn add(a: u8, b: u8) u8, without the arrow. There are no generics: fn id<T> is a parse error. The test runner on this site checks constants and does not call functions, so the lesson keeps the expected results as constants beside them.

Try it

Write a function sub in the player in either style and check the verdict stays clean.

Open the interactive lesson →
05

Module 5 · Inside a function

Names with let and var, choices with if and switch, and loops.

13

Lesson 13 of 27

Local names: let and var

You will learnWhen to use let and when var, and how a var is updated.

let a = w * h; gives a name to a value inside a function body. var i : u8 = 0; declares a name that may change, and i = i + 1; changes it. Use let when the value is computed once, var when a loop updates it. These names live only inside the function; the module level uses const.

Try it

Change let to var in area and check the verdict; then explain why let reads better there.

Open the interactive lesson →
14

Lesson 14 of 27

Choices: if, else and switch

You will learnThe forms of if the compiler accepts, the if expression, and switch with else.

if (a > b) { ... } else { ... } runs one of two blocks. The parentheses are optional: if a > b { ... } also compiles. if can be an expression too: return if (a > b) a else b; gives the larger one. switch (m) { 0 => 10, else => 20 } picks a value by matching m, and else covers every other case.

Try it

Add a case 1 => 15 to the switch in the player and check the verdict.

Open the interactive lesson →
15

Lesson 15 of 27

Loops: while and for

You will learnThe three loop forms the compiler accepts and how a range is written.

while (i < n) { i = i + 1; } repeats its block while the condition is true, and the block must move toward making it false. for i in 0..n { } walks i from 0 up to n, with n itself left out. The compiler also accepts the Zig form, for (0..4) |i| { }. A loop usually updates a var declared before it.

Try it

Work out by hand what sum_to returns for n = 4, then write it as a constant with a test.

Open the interactive lesson →
06

Module 6 · Visibility and your own types

What pub shares with other modules, and the structs and enums you declare.

16

Lesson 16 of 27

pub or private

You will learnWhat pub declares, and what the TypeScript backend writes with and without it.

pub in front of const, fn, struct or enum says other modules may use the name. Without pub the name is meant for the module itself. Today the compiler does not enforce this in the code it writes: gen-ts exports both the pub and the private constant of the lesson spec. Use pub to say what a module offers, and read the generated code before relying on privacy.

Try it

Open the ts tab of the lesson spec in the player and find both constants.

Open the interactive lesson →
17

Lesson 17 of 27

Structs

You will learnHow to declare a struct and a packed struct, and how many a module may hold.

pub struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 } declares a type with two fields. Fields are a name and a type, separated by commas. A packed struct lays its fields next to each other with no padding, the shape a hardware register has. A module may declare several structs; the lesson spec has two, and the verdict stays clean on all 7 backends.

Try it

Add a field z: i32 to Point and check which backends still compile it.

Open the interactive lesson →
18

Lesson 18 of 27

Enums

You will learnThe two ways to declare an enum and how a switch reads a value.

pub enum Color { Red, Green, Blue } names three cases. The Zig form pub const Mode = enum(u8) { Idle, Run } also fixes the type that stores a case, here u8. A switch over a value lists what each case gives and uses else for the rest. Both forms compile clean on all 7 backends in the lesson spec.

Try it

Add a fourth color to Color and update CASES_IN_COLOR so the test passes.

Open the interactive lesson →
07

Module 7 · Modules, rules and gen-ts

Reading another module, stating a rule that always holds, and a spec turned into TypeScript.

19

Lesson 19 of 27

Using other modules

You will learnHow a use line is written, and what the browser can and cannot do with it.

use base::types; names a module by its path, with :: between the parts. The parser reads it as a use declaration. The compiler in your browser has no checkout of the other files, so it does not open base::types and does not check names that come from it. The native t27c resolves imports from a repository; this lesson could not run that check here.

Try it

Find the use declaration in the parser tree of the lesson spec in the player.

Open the interactive lesson →
20

Lesson 20 of 27

Invariants and benches

You will learnHow invariant and bench blocks are written and who evaluates them.

invariant name followed by an assert states a rule of the spec that must hold for every value, not one example. bench name marks a block to time. Both compile. The test runner on this site evaluates test blocks only: it skips invariants and benches, so a false invariant passes here silently. The lesson spec repeats its invariant as a test for that reason.

Try it

Make the invariant false in the player and check that nothing on this site complains, then make the test false.

Open the interactive lesson →
21

Lesson 21 of 27

gen-ts: a spec becomes TypeScript

You will learnWhat gen-ts writes for constants and functions, and how a host program uses it.

t27c gen-ts turns each constant into an export const line that TypeScript type-checks. Functions are not emitted: the backend says it lowers declarations, not bodies. This is how this site uses specs: a generator reads a .t27 file and writes the numbers and words a page imports. The table under this lesson shows what gen-ts wrote for the lesson spec.

Try it

Add a constant to the lesson spec in the player and find its line in the ts tab.

Open the interactive lesson →
08

Module 8 · The compiler and tri

The backends t27c writes, the stages it reads a spec in, and the tri command.

22

Lesson 22 of 27

Seven backends

You will learnThe names of the 7 backends and how much code each wrote for one small spec.

The compiler in your browser has 7 backends: c, js, rust, ts, verilog, verilog_hir and zig. Each reads the same parsed spec and writes code in its language; the verilog_hir backend is written from the hardware view, HIR. The table shows the bytes each backend wrote for the lesson spec, measured with the compiler on this site. Bigger is not better: each language needs a different amount of text.

Try it

Open each backend tab of the lesson spec in the player and find the function add.

Open the interactive lesson →
23

Lesson 23 of 27

The stages of t27c

You will learnThe order of the compiler stages and what each one produced for the lesson spec.

The lexer cuts the text into tokens. The parser builds a tree of nodes. The type checker reports errors and warnings without stopping the backends. HIR is the hardware view that the verilog_hir backend is written from; the other backends read the parser's tree. The table shows the counts each stage gave for the lesson spec, measured with the compiler on this site.

Try it

Open the t27c stages widget, paste the lesson spec, and match its counts with the table.

Open the interactive lesson →
24

Lesson 24 of 27

tri: the command line

You will learnWhat tri test does, how tri hands other words to t27c, and which commands are its own.

In the gHashTag/t27 repository, scripts/tri is a small wrapper. tri test runs the conformance suite, t27c suite --repo-root .; a word tri does not know, such as gen or seal, is passed on to t27c. Its own commands include audit, recall, frontier, lesson and help. This lesson read the script and did not run it: native t27c is built on a Linux machine, and this course does not run it on yours.

Try it

Read the table and say which commands go to t27c and which stay inside tri.

09

Module 9 · Errors, a program, what next

Reading a compiler error, one small complete program, and the course to take next.

25

Lesson 25 of 27

Reading compiler errors

You will learnHow to read the line and column of an error, using four real mistakes.

A parse error says where the parser was, near which line, and the token it did not expect, with a line and a column. A type error names the constant and why its value does not fit. Read the position first, then look one token to the left: the mistake is often just before the place the parser stopped. The table shows what the compiler on this site answered for four small mistakes.

Try it

Make each of the four mistakes in the player and match the line and column with the table.

Open the interactive lesson →
26

Lesson 26 of 27

A small complete program

You will learnHow the pieces of this course make one spec that becomes a circuit.

The lesson spec has a module line, a width constant, test values and on_comb, a function of two u8 inputs. gen-verilog turns it into a module whose ports are a clock, a reset and an enable, the two 8-bit inputs a and b, a ready output and the 8-bit output result. An assign line sets result from on_comb, so the sum itself waits for no clock edge. The tests check the example sums as constants; the site runner does not call on_comb, so the check of the circuit itself is left to a simulator.

Try it

Open the verilog tab of the lesson spec in the player and find the input, output and assign lines.

Open the interactive lesson →

Lesson 27 of 27

Where to go next

You will learnWhich course to take next, and what each one adds to the basics.

You can now read a spec: its module line, constants, types, functions, tests and the code its backends write. Course 1 follows a spec onto an Artix-7 FPGA: synthesis, placement, timing and a bitstream checked on a board. Course 2 builds number formats for AI in t27, from OCP MX blocks to a ternary network. Both courses have 27 lessons and open a spec in every one.

TRI CLAW

The agent behind t27, in Telegram and on GitHub

TRI CLAW is the project's agent: it writes and checks .t27 specs with you. Three ways to use it.

  • Free, with your own key

    Add your own API key (NVIDIA or z.ai today) and the agent runs on it. Add more keys any time.

    Add a key in Telegram ↗

  • We do it for you

    No keys to keep: join the club in our Telegram bot and the agent runs on ours. The bot shows the price before you pay.

    Join the club in Telegram ↗

  • On GitHub

    TRI CLAW is also a GitHub App, built to check the .t27 specs a pull request changes. It is not open to other repositories yet.

    Read about TRI CLAW ↗
